question: Which statement best describes What SSG actually does?
options: You can explicitly opt a route segment into static rendering with a route segment config export. This guarantees the route is built statically (and uncached data is treated as empty/cached), which is handy to document intent or to prevent accidental dynamic rendering.

At build time, Next.js runs your Server Component, fetches its (cacheable) data, renders React to HTML, and writes static files. Those files are pushed to a CDN and served instantly to every visitor without any server work per request. In the App Router this is the default for routes whose data is cacheable.

In the App Router a plain fetch is cached by default, so a route that only uses such fetches is statically generated automatically — you don't opt in. The page is built once and the result is reused for every request, which is why SSG is the framework's default for stable, shareable content.

For a dynamic segment like blog/[slug], you tell Next.js which paths to pre-build by exporting generateStaticParams, which returns the list of param values. Next then statically generates one HTML file per slug at build time, so every known page is CDN-fast.

Those files are pushed to a CDN and served instantly to every visitor without any server work per request. In the App Router this is the default for routes whose data is cacheable.
